newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian data backs stronger economy view.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian data backs stronger economy view.

text.p: The pace of economic activity in Australia appears to have stepped up a notch in the early stages of 1997, confirming the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) steady outlook for interest rates, economists said.
Data released on Tuesday, the same day as the RBA board met, showed that January retail trade rose 2.7 percent and building approvals for the same month were up 10.4 percent.
"It's just continuing the stronger run of data which has come in at the stronger end of expectations over the last month or so," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.
The retail sales rise was the largest since March 1994, and reversed the weakness seen in the later stages of 1996. Retail sales are now just under their July 1996 level.
Building approvals are at their highest level since May 1995, and in annual terms are up 22.5 percent.

"I think we already had plenty of indicators the economy was picking up in the first quarter," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell senior economist Bruce Hockman said, adding the anecdotes on retail trade suggested it had remained strong into February.
"So not only are we off to a good start in January, there may be some follow through in February," he said.

While the building approvals data had been volatile since the second half of 1996, with three rises since July of more than 10 percent interspersed with four falls, the data has been showing a gradual improvement.
The average monthly level of approvals was 600 higher in the second half of the year than the first, and the January rise was a further sign of improving conditions in the housing sector.
"With housing affordability at record highs, the building industry is entering a strong period of solid upswing," Axiom Funds Management senior economist Matthew Drennan said.
"Traditionally the housing sector has had strong spin-off effects on employment and retail sales -- two of the greatest areas of concern to the Reserve Bank," he said.

Two weeks ago, the RBA said that while the pace of economic growth remained moderate, "the data becoming available over the past couple of months have been firmer, on average, than those received during the second half of the 1996."
"The outlook now is for stronger growth during 1997 than that experienced through 1996," the RBA continued, a sentiment that was finding broad support in the market.
This, combined with some caution over the wages outlook meant the RBA saw "current monetary policy settings as broadly appropriate for the time being."

Accordingly, expectations of a rate cut to follow the three in the second half of last year have almost disappeared, with a tightening, possibly by the end of the year, now seen as the most likely next move in rates. No change is expected to follow Tuesday's meeting.
"I think they would be looking to see whether the economy is passing its low point, and that certainly appears to be the case," ANZ Bank senior Treasury economist David De Garis said.

He added that the economy was still well within its growth potential, and the inflation outlook was very good, meaning that while a cut from the current offical rate of 6.00 percent was not likely, neither was there a need to push them higher.

"So I don't think there's any necessity for the Reserve Bank to change interest rates in either direction just yet, and probably hold them where they are for another six to nine months at least," he said.
